item.title: Annotate Command (annotate)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: annotate

Use annotate to add, change, or remove annotations after the backup command creates a backup.

Command Options

Backup Annotation Option (--annotation)

Annotate backup with user-defined key/value pairs.

Attach informative key/value pairs to the backup. Repeat this option to attach multiple annotations.

When --set specifies a backup, the info command includes its annotations in text output. JSON output always includes annotations.

item.title: Cluster / Instance
item.description:
Select instance and cluster types that meet your requirements.

Pigsty supports several PostgreSQL instance and cluster types:

  • Primary: Define a single instance cluster.
  • Replica: Define a basic HA cluster with one primary and one replica.
  • Offline: Define an instance dedicated to OLAP/ETL/interactive queries
  • Sync Standby: Enable synchronous commit to ensure no data loss.
  • Quorum Commit: Use quorum sync commit for a higher consistency level.
  • Standby Cluster: Clone an existing cluster and follow it
  • Delayed Cluster: Clone an existing cluster for emergency data recovery
  • Citus Cluster: Define a Citus distributed database cluster

Primary

The simplest cluster contains one primary instance:

“PostgreSQL In Great STYle”: Postgres, Infras, Graphics, Service, Toolbox, it’s all Yours.

—— Battery-Included, Local-First PostgreSQL Distribution as a Free & Open-Source RDS Alternative

Free & Open Source Local First Production Ready

GitHub | Demo | Blog | Discuss | Discord | DeepWiki | Roadmap | Chinese Docs

Getting Started

item.title: Dynamic Configuration Settings
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/dynamic_configuration.html

Dynamic configuration is stored in the DCS (Distributed Configuration Store) and applied on all cluster nodes.

Change dynamic configuration with patronictl_edit_config or the Patroni REST API.

  • loop_wait: the number of seconds the loop will sleep. Default value: 10, minimum possible value: 1
  • ttl: leader lock TTL, in seconds. This is the interval before automatic failover can start. Default: 30. Minimum: 20.
  • retry_timeout: timeout for DCS and PostgreSQL operation retries (in seconds). DCS or network issues shorter than this will not cause Patroni to demote the leader. Default value: 10, minimum possible value: 3
Warning

when changing values of loop_wait, retry_timeout, or ttl you have to follow the rule:

loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl

item.title: Features
item.description:
“PostgreSQL In Great STYle”: Postgres, Infras, Graphics, Service, Toolbox, it’s all Yours.

—— Battery-included, local-first PostgreSQL distribution, open-source RDS alternative

Value Propositions

  • Extensibility: Powerful extensions out of the box: deep integration of PostGIS, TimescaleDB, Citus, PGVector, 600 plugins, and 12 PG kernels.
  • Reliability: Quickly create high-availability, self-healing PostgreSQL clusters with built-in point-in-time recovery, access control, a self-signed CA, and TLS.
  • Observability: Prometheus and Grafana provide a modular monitoring stack that can operate independently. See the Gallery and Demo.
  • Availability: Deliver stable, reliable, auto-routed, transaction-pooled, read-write separated high-performance database services, with flexible access modes via HAProxy, Pgbouncer, and VIP.
  • Maintainability: Easy to use, Infrastructure as Code, Management SOPs, auto-tuning, local software repository, Vagrant sandbox and OpenTofu templates, zero-downtime migration solutions.
  • Composability: Modular architecture design, reusable Infra, various optional modules: Redis, Silo object storage, ETCD, DuckDB, Docker, Supabase.

Overview

Pigsty is a local, open-source alternative to PostgreSQL RDS:

item.title: News
item.description:
Source: https://pgbackrest.org/news.html

pgBackRest 2.59.2 Released

September 27, 2026

The pgBackRest community released pgBackRest 2.59.2. This backup and restore solution supports PostgreSQL databases and workloads of all sizes.

pgBackRest provides these backup and recovery features: parallel backup and restore; full, differential, incremental, and block incremental backups; and multiple repositories. It also supports delta restore, parallel asynchronous archiving, malware/ransomware protection, per-file checksums, and validation of enabled page checksums during backup. Other features include multiple compression types, encryption, partial/failed backup resume, standby backups, tablespaces, and links. Storage options include S3, Azure, GCS, and SFTP. pgBackRest also supports backup expiration, local or remote operation through SSH or TLS, and flexible configuration.

item.title: Parameter Optimization Policy
item.description:
Pigsty provides four parameter templates for different workloads. Select a template with pg_conf.

  • tiny.yml: Optimized for small nodes, VMs, and demos (the template is labeled for 1-3 cores)
  • oltp.yml: Optimized for OLTP workloads and latency-sensitive applications (4C8GB+) (default template)
  • olap.yml: Optimized for OLAP workloads and throughput (4C8G+)
  • crit.yml: Optimized for data consistency and critical applications (4C8G+)

The following sections describe the optimization settings for these four templates.

Memory Parameter Tuning

Pigsty detects the system’s memory size. It uses this value to set the maximum number of connections and memory-related parameters.

item.title: YAML Configuration Settings
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/yaml_configuration.html

Global/Universal

  • thread_pool_size: thread pool size for asynchronous tasks and REST API communication with other members during leader races or failsafe checks. Minimum: 5. Default: 5.
  • thread_stack_size: stack size for Patroni threads. Use a multiple of 64kB. Minimum: 64kB. Patroni default: 512kB.
  • name: the name of the host. Must be unique for the cluster. The value __patroni_strict_sync_replica_placeholder__ is reserved for internal use by Patroni and cannot be used as a node name.
  • namespace: path within the configuration store where Patroni will keep information about the cluster. Default value: “/service”
  • scope: cluster name

item.title: Archive Get Command (archive-get)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: archive-get

PostgreSQL uses this command to restore a backup or perform PITR. It can also use the command instead of streaming to keep a replica current. PostgreSQL needs WAL segments for recovery and replica maintenance.

With multiple repositories, pgBackRest searches for WAL in priority order, such as repo1, then repo2. Usually, give faster or cheaper storage higher priority. If --repo specifies a repository, pgBackRest searches only that repository.

item.title: Configuration: pgbouncer.ini
item.description:
Source: https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html · 1.26.0 source

Description

The configuration file uses INI format. Section names appear between [ and ]. Lines beginning with ; or # are comments and are ignored. Elsewhere in a line, these characters have no special meaning.

Generic settings

logfile

Specifies the log file. For daemonization (-d), either this or syslog need to be set.

item.title: History
item.description:
Historical Origins

Pigsty began in 2018-2019 at Tantan. Tantan is a dating app similar to Tinder in China, later acquired by Momo. Its founding engineering team was Swedish, and its startup culture followed a Nordic model.

Tantan used PostgreSQL and Go as its core stack. Its architecture followed Instagram and centered on PostgreSQL. It served several million daily active users, millions of TPS, and hundreds of TB of data. The data layer used only PostgreSQL. PG stored procedures implemented almost all business logic, including 100ms recommendation algorithms. This was arguably one of China’s most complex large-scale PostgreSQL deployments at the time.

item.title: Kernel Version
item.description:
Choosing a “kernel” in Pigsty means determining the PostgreSQL major version, mode/distribution, packages to install, and tuning templates to load.

The Pigsty v4.5 source supports PostgreSQL 14-18 and uses 18 by default. Use the following configuration settings to select a kernel.

Major Version and Packages

  • pg_version: Select the PostgreSQL major version. The default is 18. Pigsty maps the version to the correct package name prefix.
  • pg_packages: Select core packages with package aliases. The default, pgsql-main pgsql-common, includes the kernel, Patroni, PgBouncer, pgBackRest, and other common tools.
  • pg_extensions: Select additional extension packages. Aliases are supported. The default is empty, which installs only core dependencies.
all:
 vars:
 pg_version: 18
 pg_packages: [ pgsql-main, pgsql-common ]
 pg_extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, pgvector, pgml ]

During installation, Ansible downloads packages for pg_version=18 and installs extension files on the system. Database initialization scripts can then run CREATE EXTENSION.

item.title: OLTP Template
item.description:
oltp.yml is Pigsty’s default configuration template for online transaction processing (OLTP). It is designed for CPUs with 4-128 cores and provides high concurrency, low latency, and high throughput.

Pair with node_tune = oltp for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the OLTP template for:

  • E-commerce: Order processing, inventory, user transactions
  • Social apps: User feeds, messaging, following relationships
  • Gaming backends: Player data, leaderboards, game state
  • SaaS applications: Multi-tenant business systems
  • Web apps: CRUD-intensive workloads

Workload characteristics:

item.title: Archive Push Command (archive-push)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: archive-push

This command accepts a WAL segment from PostgreSQL. It archives the segment in each repository defined by an indexed repo-path option. See Repository for configuration details. The archive-async value determines whether pgBackRest immediately archives the segment or stores it locally first. With multiple repositories, archive-push attempts to write to as many as possible.

Configure PostgreSQL to call archive-push. See the example in Configure Archiving.

Command Options

Asynchronous Archiving Option (--archive-async)

Push/get WAL segments asynchronously.

item.title: Environment Configuration Settings
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ENVIRONMENT.html

System environment variables can override some Patroni configuration file parameters. This page lists all supported variables. Environment values always take precedence over file values.

Global/Universal

  • PATRONI_CONFIGURATION: sets the complete Patroni configuration through PATRONI_CONFIGURATION. Patroni then ignores all other environment variables.
  • PATRONI_THREAD_POOL_SIZE: thread pool size for asynchronous tasks and REST API communication with other members during leader races or failsafe checks. Minimum: 5. Default: 5.
  • PATRONI_THREAD_STACK_SIZE: stack size for Patroni threads. Use a multiple of 64kB. Minimum: 64kB. Patroni default: 512kB.
  • PATRONI_NAME: name of the node where the current instance of Patroni is running. Must be unique for the cluster. The value __patroni_strict_sync_replica_placeholder__ is reserved for internal use by Patroni and cannot be used as a node name.
  • PATRONI_NAMESPACE: path within the configuration store where Patroni will keep information about the cluster. Default value: “/service”
  • PATRONI_SCOPE: cluster name
  • PG_MALLOC_ARENA_MAX: custom value for MALLOC_ARENA_MAX environment variable for postmaster process. If not set, postmaster will inherit MALLOC_ARENA_MAX value.

Log

  • PATRONI_LOG_TYPE: sets the format of logs. Can be either plain or json. To use json format, you must have the jsonlogger installed. The default value is plain.
  • PATRONI_LOG_LEVEL: sets the general logging level. Default value is INFO (see the docs for Python logging)
  • PATRONI_LOG_TRACEBACK_LEVEL: sets the level where tracebacks will be visible. Default value is ERROR. Set it to DEBUG if you want to see tracebacks only if you enable PATRONI_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FORMAT: log format. For plain logs, use a string. For json, use a string or a list of LogRecord attributes. In lists, use field names without %( and ). To rename a field, use a dictionary with the original field as key and the output name as value. Default: %(asctime)s %(levelname)s: %(message)s.
  • PATRONI_LOG_DATEFORMAT: sets the datetime formatting string. (see the formatTime() documentation)
  • PATRONI_LOG_STATIC_FIELDS: add additional fields to the log. This option is only available when the log type is set to json. Example PATRONI_LOG_STATIC_FIELDS="{app: patroni}"
  • PATRONI_LOG_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE: maximum internal log queue size. Patroni writes records to an in-memory queue. A separate thread reads them and writes to stderr or a file. The default 1000 records retain approximately 1h20m of logs.
  • PATRONI_LOG_DIR: application log directory. It must exist and be writable by the Patroni user. By default, Patroni retains four 25MB files. Adjust retention with PATRONI_LOG_FILE_NUM and PATRONI_LOG_FILE_SIZE.
  • PATRONI_LOG_MODE: Permissions for log files (for example, 0644). If not specified, permissions will be set based on the current umask value.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FILE_NUM: The number of application logs to retain.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FILE_SIZE: Size of patroni.log file (in bytes) that triggers a log rolling.
  • PATRONI_LOG_LOGGERS: Redefine logging level per python module. Example PATRONI_LOG_LOGGERS="{patroni.postmaster: WARNING, urllib3: DEBUG}"
  • PATRONI_LOG_DEDUPLICATE_HEARTBEAT_LOGS: suppresses consecutive identical heartbeat messages when true. Default: false.
Warning

HA loop timing helps diagnose failovers caused by exhausted resources and similar problems. With PATRONI_LOG_DEDUPLICATE_HEARTBEAT_LOGS set to true, loop execution produces no log unless the leader changes. These diagnostics are then unavailable in the logs.

item.title: OLAP Template
item.description:
olap.yml is optimized for online analytical processing (OLAP) on CPUs with 4-128 cores. It supports large queries, high parallelism, relaxed timeouts, and aggressive vacuum.

Pair with node_tune = olap for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the OLAP template for:

  • Data warehouses: Historical data storage, multidimensional analysis
  • BI reports: Complex report queries, dashboard data sources
  • ETL processing: Data extraction, transformation, loading
  • Data analysis: Ad-hoc queries, data exploration
  • HTAP mixed workloads: Analytical replicas

Workload characteristics:

item.title: Package Alias
item.description:
PostgreSQL package names differ between operating systems:

  • EL systems (RHEL/Rocky/Alma/…) use formats like pgvector_18, postgis36_18*
  • Debian/Ubuntu systems use formats like postgresql-18-pgvector, postgresql-18-postgis-3

Without aliases, you need different naming rules for each system. You must also include the correct PostgreSQL version in the names.

Package Alias

Use a Package Alias to specify the same component on different platforms. Pigsty converts it to the correct package names:

item.title: Patroni configuration
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/patroni_configuration.html

There are 3 types of Patroni configuration:

  • Global dynamic configuration.
    These options are stored in the DCS (Distributed Configuration Store) and apply to all nodes. Change them at any time with patronictl_edit_config or the REST API. Changes outside startup configuration apply asynchronously on each node’s next wake-up cycle, followed by a reload. Changed PostgreSQL parameters with postmaster context require a restart. Patroni sets pending_restart in members.data JSON for these nodes. Node status also shows "restart_pending": true.

  • Local configuration file (patroni.yml).
    Local options override dynamic configuration. To reload patroni.yml without restarting Patroni, send SIGHUP, send POST /reload, or run patronictl_reload. Local configuration can be one YAML file or a directory. Patroni loads all YAML files in a directory in sorted order. If several files define a key, the last file takes precedence.

  • Environment configuration.
    Environment variables can set or override some local parameters. Use them in dynamic environments where some values are unknown in advance. For example, the external IP address may be unknown inside docker.

item.title: Backup Command (backup)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: backup

With multiple repositories, pgBackRest backs up to the highest priority repository, such as repo1. Use --repo to select another repository.

pgBackRest has no built-in scheduler. Use cron or another scheduler to run it.

See Perform a Backup for more details and examples.

Command Options

Backup Annotation Option (--annotation)

Annotate backup with user-defined key/value pairs.

Attach informative key/value pairs to the backup. Repeat this option to attach multiple annotations.

item.title: Command Reference
item.description:
Source: https://pgbackrest.org/command.html

Introduction

Commands execute pgBackRest functions. Each command page lists every applicable option, including options shared with other commands. The lists also include options that you can set in pgbackrest.conf.

Use the reset- prefix on the command line to reset a non-boolean option from pgbackrest.conf to its default. For example, use this feature to restore a backup directly on a repository host. Normally, pgBackRest detects the remote database host and reports an error because remote restores are not supported. Add --reset-pg1-host to ignore the remote database host and restore locally. You might also need --pg1-path to select a path other than the database host path.

item.title: CRIT Template
item.description:
crit.yml is for transactional workloads with increased consistency and audit requirements. It forces data checksums and Patroni strict synchronous mode. It also adds connection logging and adjusts selected WAL, timeout, and parallel-query parameters.

The template increases write latency and may block writes when no synchronous replica is available. Before use, confirm consistency objectives, failure domains, client commit settings, and availability requirements.

Also evaluate node_tune: crit. You can select host tuning and database parameters independently.

item.title: Patroni REST API
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/rest_api.html

Patroni uses its REST API during leader races. patronictl uses it for failovers, switchovers, reinitialization, restarts, and reloads. HAProxy and other load balancers use it for HTTP health checks. Monitoring systems can also use it. This page lists the available endpoints.

Health check endpoints

Health check GET requests return an HTTP status code and a JSON document with node status. Use HEAD or OPTIONS instead of GET if you do not need JSON.

item.title: User/Role
item.description:
In this document, “user” refers to a logical object within a database cluster created with CREATE USER/ROLE.

In PostgreSQL, users belong to the database cluster, rather than a specific database. Create business users before you create business databases.

Pigsty defines roles and users through two config parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: Define globally shared roles and users
  • pg_users: Define business users and roles at cluster level

The first parameter defines roles and users shared across the environment. The second defines business roles and users for one cluster. Both parameters use arrays of user definition objects. Pigsty creates users and roles in array order. Thus, a later user can belong to an earlier role.

item.title: Check Command (check)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: check

The check command validates pgBackRest and archive_command configuration for the specified stanza. It checks backup and archive settings for all repositories and databases configured on the current host. It detects configuration errors, especially archive errors that leave backups incomplete because required WAL segments never reached the archive. Run it on the PostgreSQL or repository host. You can also run it on a standby, but then it checks only repository configuration. A standby cannot execute pg_switch_xlog()/pg_switch_wal().

item.title: Configuration Reference
item.description:
Introduction

You can configure pgBackRest entirely with command-line parameters. For complex installations or many options, a configuration file is more practical. Its default location is /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf. If that file is absent, pgBackRest checks the old default, /etc/pgbackrest.conf.

The following option types are used:

String: A text string, commonly an identifier, password, etc.

Command line example: --stanza=demo
Configuration file example: repo1-cipher-pass=zWaf6XtpjIVZC5444yXB...

Path: Identify a location in a directory structure. Paths must start with /. They cannot contain double // and should not end with /.

item.title: Database
item.description:
In this document, “database” refers to a logical object within a database cluster created with CREATE DATABASE.

A PostgreSQL cluster can serve multiple databases at the same time. Define the required databases in the Pigsty cluster configuration.

Pigsty customizes the template1 database with default schemas, extensions, and privileges. New databases inherit these settings from template1. Use template to select another template for instant database cloning.

By default, Pigsty adds each application database to the PgBouncer connection pool with a 1:1 mapping. pg_exporter discovers application databases automatically to monitor their objects. Pigsty also registers all databases as PostgreSQL data sources in Grafana on every INFRA node for PGCAT dashboards.

item.title: patronictl
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/patronictl.html

The patronictl command-line interface communicates with the Patroni REST API and the DCS. Use it for cluster operations, interactively or in scripts.

Configuration

patronictl uses 3 sections of the configuration:

  • ctl: REST API authentication and server identity verification. See ctl settings.
  • restapi: fallback settings when ctl does not supply REST API authentication or server verification. patronictl uses restapi.authentication if ctl.authentication is absent, and restapi.cafile if ctl.cacert is absent. See REST API settings.
  • DCS, such as etcd: DCS connection and authentication settings.

Supply these options through environment variables or a configuration file. See the corresponding sections in Environment Configuration Settings and YAML Configuration Settings.

item.title: TINY Template
item.description:
tiny.yml is optimized for micro instances and environments with limited resources. It is designed for CPUs with 1-3 cores. It minimizes resource use, limits memory allocation, and disables parallel queries.

Pair with node_tune = tiny for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the TINY template for:

  • Dev/test: Local development, CI/CD testing
  • Low-spec VMs: 1-2 core CPU, 1-4GB RAM cloud instances
  • Edge computing: Raspberry Pi, embedded devices
  • Demos: Quick Pigsty experience
  • Personal projects: Resource-limited blogs, small apps

Resource constraints:

item.title: Expire Command (expire)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: expire

pgBackRest rotates full backups according to a count or time period. Count-based retention keeps a specified number of backups, regardless of their creation times. Differential retention uses a count, but a differential always expires with its parent full backup. Incremental backups have no independent expiration policy. They expire with their parent full or differential backup. See Full Backup Retention and Differential Backup Retention for details and examples.

By default, pgBackRest keeps archived WAL for unexpired backups. You can change this per repository with retention-archive options, but this is not recommended. See Archive Retention for details and examples.

item.title: HBA Rules
item.description:
Overview

HBA (Host-Based Authentication) controls who can connect to a database, from which source, and with which authentication method. For the authentication model and default rules, see Authentication. Pigsty manages HBA rules through pg_default_hba_rules and pg_hba_rules.

Pigsty generates these files during cluster initialization or HBA refresh:

Config File Path Description
PostgreSQL HBA /pg/data/pg_hba.conf PostgreSQL server HBA rules
PgBouncer HBA /etc/pgbouncer/pgb_hba.conf Connection pool HBA rules

HBA rules are controlled by these parameters:

item.title: Release Notes
item.description:
Introduction

pgBackRest release numbers have major and minor parts. A major release may break compatibility with the previous major release. However, v2 releases fully support v1 repositories and accept all v1 options. Minor releases can add features and bug fixes. They do not change the repository format and aim to preserve option names and behavior. See the v1 documentation.

A release can include “Additional Notes”. These cover only documentation or test-suite changes and do not directly affect the pgBackRest codebase.

item.title: Access Control
item.description:
Access control combines roles, object privileges, database ACLs, and HBA. This page describes configuration parameters. For design and boundaries, see Access Control Concepts.

Pigsty provides a compact ACL model described by these parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: system roles and system users.
  • pg_users: application users and roles.
  • pg_default_privileges: default privileges on objects created by managed administrators and owners.
  • pg_revoke_public, pg_default_schemas, and pg_default_extensions: default behavior for template1.

Manage these parameters together with HBA and database definitions to produce reproducible access-control configuration.

item.title: Changelog
item.description:
Source: https://www.pgbouncer.org/changelog.html · 1.26.0 source

PgBouncer 1.26.x

2026-09-23 - PgBouncer 1.26.0 - “Ignore all previous search_path”

  • Security
    • Fix CVE-2026-19888: PgBouncer before 1.26.0 did not check that the SCRAM client-final-message contained a nonce. An unauthenticated remote attacker could crash PgBouncer by sending a client-final-message without one. This also applies to users that do not exist, because PgBouncer runs a mock SCRAM exchange for those. This bug has existed since SCRAM support was added in PgBouncer 1.11.0.
    • Fix CVE-2026-6668: Before 1.26.0, integer overflow in packet buffer growth could make PgBouncer loop indefinitely. This required a large amount of data in one packet buffer. With default max_packet_size, an unauthenticated client could trigger it. Because PgBouncer is single-threaded, it stopped serving all clients until the process was killed.
    • Fix CVE-2026-6669: Before 1.26.0, PgBouncer accepted an unbounded SCRAM iteration count from servers. A malicious or compromised PostgreSQL server could force unlimited work during one login. This blocked service for all other clients and databases. The iteration count must now be at most 1000000.
  • Features
    • Track all parameters that PostgreSQL reports by default. These include search_path on PostgreSQL 18+ and default_transaction_read_only on PostgreSQL 14+. Previously, SET search_path or SET default_transaction_read_only = true in transaction pooling affected later clients that used the same server connection. (#1580, #1573)
    • Add pool_idle_timeout to remove pools unused for a configured period. This helps when many users connect infrequently and pool counts otherwise grow without limit. The default disables this setting because pool removal also removes its statistics. (#1491)
    • Allow query_wait_timeout to be configured per user and per database. (#1449)
    • Add client_login_count stat to SHOW STATS, which counts successful client logins. This makes it possible to detect clients that churn connections. (#1457)
    • Send PgBouncer-specific ParameterStatus messages at client login: pgbouncer.version, pgbouncer.pool_mode, and pgbouncer.max_prepared_statements. Clients and drivers can use these to detect PgBouncer and adjust their behavior. (#1490)
    • Add login_notify_message setting. When set, its value is sent to clients as a NOTICE message after they log in. This can be used to make it clear to clients that they are connected through PgBouncer instead of directly to PostgreSQL. (#1488)
    • Add support for building PgBouncer with meson, including a Windows build using the UCRT64 environment. Autoconf builds continue to be supported. (#1524, #1426, #1568, #1585, #1602, #1607)
    • Add a logo. (#1609)
  • Changes
    • Remove the deprecated online restart (-R, aka takeover) functionality, together with the SHOW FDS and SUSPEND admin commands that only existed to support it. Use rolling restarts with so_reuseport instead. (#1581)
    • Increase the maximum length of passwords to 65535 bytes, matching libpq. (#1310, #1520)
    • Treat a NULL user name returned by auth_query the same as no rows being returned, instead of treating it as an error. (#1569)
    • Accept SET extra_float_digits on the admin database, which newer PostgreSQL JDBC drivers send during connection setup. (#1550)
    • Allow mkauth.py to write to stdout by passing - as the output file. (#1514)
    • Stop logging noisy errors on unexpected EOF from clients when built against OpenSSL 3. (#1507)
    • Include the underlying system error in TLS error messages when built against OpenSSL 3. (#1492)
    • Require a C11 compiler. (#1417)
    • Log which limit caused a server connection to be evicted. The disconnect reason is now evicted for max_db_connections, evicted for pool_size or evicted for max_user_connections instead of the bare evicted. (#1597)
  • Fixes
    • Fix late COPY messages causing pool exhaustion in transaction pooling mode. This also makes COPY work outside of an explicit transaction in transaction pooling mode. (#1471)
    • Fix LDAP authentication failures with long DNs by increasing the maximum LDAP URL length. (#1497)
    • Fix SCRAM pass-through corruption of cached forced-user credentials. This caused server login failures because the real server rejected the SCRAM proof. (#1612)
    • Fix SCRAM pass-through with stored SCRAM secrets after server reconnection. It failed with “password is SCRAM secret but client authentication did not provide SCRAM keys”. (#1504, bug introduced in 1.25.1)
    • Fix use-after-free crash when a replication client disconnects while its server connection is still logging in. (#1577)
    • Fix idle server eviction for replication clients when the pool is full. Previously, one replication client could evict every idle server instead of one. No eviction occurred when reserve pools or cancel requests made the server count exceed pool_size. (#1597)
    • Fix stalled TLS connections when a packet straddles the packet buffer boundary, for example a SET application_name with a long value. (#1531)
    • Fix prepared statement responses being sent in the wrong order when a batch mixes Parse and Close messages without a Sync in between. (#1555)
    • Fix parameters listed in track_extra_parameters that are not reported by the server causing incorrect behaviour when a client sets them in its startup packet. (#1576)
    • Fix login failures when the server splits its login packets across multiple TCP packets, for example when there is another proxy between PgBouncer and PostgreSQL. (#1446)
    • Fix query_timeout closing connections when no query was in flight. (#1395)
    • Fix sending a duplicate NegotiateProtocolVersion message when no server was available right away. (#1460)
    • Fix pool_size column in SHOW USERS showing a value for users that do not have one configured. (#1489)
    • Fix error message for ENABLE admin command. (#1308)
    • Fix compilation against future OpenSSL versions that make struct asn1_string_st opaque. (#1440)
    • Prevent the compiler from optimizing away the erasure of sensitive cryptographic data from the stack. (#1508)
    • Fix linking of pgbevent.dll with clang on Windows. (#1571)
    • Fix paths of root-level files in the release tarball, which were stored as pgbouncer-X.Y.Z/./configure instead of pgbouncer-X.Y.Z/configure. (#1549)
    • Fix a memory leak when reading track_extra_parameters from the config. (#1510)
    • Fix a memory leak for every startup packet that contained a protocol extension parameter (_pq_. prefix), which could be triggered by unauthenticated clients. (#1540)

PgBouncer 1.25.x

2026-05-08 - PgBouncer 1.25.2 - “Human touch with fresh twist in title race full of uncertainties”

item.title: Frequently Asked Questions
item.description:
Introduction

These answers cover specific questions that the User Guide and references might not cover. If your issue is absent, check the pgBackRest Issues List in GitHub.

What if I get the “could not find WAL segment” error?

This error has several possible causes:

  • misconfigured archive_command
  • misconfigured pgBackRest configuration files
  • network or permissions issue
  • third party product (e.g. S3, Swift or Minio) configuration issue
  • large amount of WAL queueing to be archived

Check these items:

item.title: Help Command (help)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: help

Help has three levels. With no command, pgBackRest shows general help. With a command, such as pgbackrest help backup, it shows the command description and valid options. Add an option, such as pgbackrest help backup type, to show its full description for that command.

Command Options

Display Help Option (--help)

Display help.

Show help even without the help command. This overrides --version.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
You can set PostgreSQL parameters at several levels with different scopes and priorities. Pigsty supports four levels, from global to local:

Level Scope Configuration Method Storage Location
Cluster All instances in cluster Patroni DCS / Tuning Templates etcd + postgresql.conf
Instance Single PG instance pg_parameters / ALTER SYSTEM postgresql.auto.conf
Database All sessions in a DB pg_databases[].parameters pg_db_role_setting
User All sessions of a user pg_users[].parameters pg_db_role_setting

Priority from low to high: Cluster < Instance < Database < User < Session (SET command). Higher priority settings override lower ones.

item.title: Info Command (info)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: info

The info command reports on one stanza or all stanzas. By default, text output summarizes backups for the requested stanzas. The text format can change in any release.

For machine-readable output, use --output=json. JSON includes much more information than text output. Its format stays stable unless a bug requires a change.

Use --detail-level=progress to show only progress and reduce execution time. This skips all checks except stanza availability.

item.title: Frequently Asked Questions
item.description:
Source: https://www.pgbouncer.org/faq.html

How to connect to PgBouncer?

PgBouncer acts as a Postgres server. Configure your client to use the PgBouncer port.

How to load-balance queries between several servers?

PgBouncer supports comma-separated hosts in a database connection string. With load_balance_hosts=round-robin, new server connections use each host in turn. For example:

[databases]
app = host=pg1,pg2 port=5432 dbname=app load_balance_hosts=round-robin

You can also use external tools:

item.title: Repository Get Command (repo-get)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: repo-get

This command works like Unix cat on any supported repository type. Supply a fully qualified file name. It mainly supports administration, investigation, and testing. A normal pgBackRest setup does not require it.

For an encrypted repository, repo-get decrypts the file automatically. It does not decompress files. Pipe the output through the appropriate decompression command, such as gzip -d.

With multiple repositories, this command uses the highest priority repository, such as repo1. Use --repo to select another repository.

item.title: pig
item.description:
pig manages PostgreSQL packages, local database services, and Pigsty deployments. Choose a command below for your task. Use pig COMMAND --help to see the options supported by your installed program.

  • pig repo: manage software repositories
  • pig ext: manage PostgreSQL extensions
  • pig build: build extensions from source
  • pig install: install packages with the native package manager and translate PostgreSQL aliases
  • pig sty: manage Pigsty installation and Grafana dashboards
  • pig inventory: inspect, edit, validate, and exchange the Pigsty inventory
  • pig do: run Pigsty administration playbook tasks
  • pig pe: access pg_exporter metrics and configuration
  • pig pg: manage local PostgreSQL servers
  • pig pt: run patronictl transparently with service and config helpers
  • pig pb: manage pgBackRest backup and restore
  • pig pitr: run the full PITR workflow
  • pig context: output an environment context snapshot for humans and agents
  • pig license: issue and verify Pigsty licenses
  • pig status / update / version: inspect environment status, upgrade pig, and print version information

Global options

Option Purpose
-h, --help Show help
-H, --home PATH Select the Pigsty installation directory
-i, --inventory PATH Select the inventory
-o, --output FORMAT Output format: text (default), json, yaml, or json-pretty
--debug Enable debug logging
--log-level LEVEL Log level: debug, info (default), warn, error, fatal, or panic
--log-path PATH Write logs to a file; the default is the terminal

PIG-owned results support structured output. Raw-content commands such as inventory show and passthrough commands such as pt list retain their native output. See the command reference for details.

item.title: Repository List Command (repo-ls)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: repo-ls

This command works like Unix ls on any supported repository type. Supply an absolute path or a path relative to --repo-path. It mainly supports administration, investigation, and testing. A normal pgBackRest setup does not require it.

Default text output prints one file name per line. Use --output=json for JSON output.

With multiple repositories, this command uses the highest priority repository, such as repo1. Use --repo to select another repository.

item.title: pig repo
item.description:
pig repo manages Linux package repositories. Use it to add or remove APT/YUM/DNF sources, refresh indexes, and create or extract offline bundles. repo create also supports macOS through SOW.

Command Description Notes
repo list Print available repositories and modules
repo info Show repository details
repo status Show current repository status
repo add Add repositories Requires sudo or root
repo set Clear, overwrite, and update repositories Requires sudo or root
repo rm Remove repositories Requires sudo or root
repo update Update repository cache Requires sudo or root
repo create Create local YUM/APT repository Linux: sudo/root; macOS: current user
repo cache Create offline package from local repo Requires sudo or root
repo boot Bootstrap repository from offline package Requires sudo or root
repo reload Refresh repository catalog

Quick Start

On a host with working OS repositories, add the PostgreSQL repositories and refresh their indexes:

item.title: Restore Command (restore)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: restore

By default, restore selects the latest backup from the first repository that has backups. See Quick Start - Restore a Backup. The repository order comes from pgbackrest.conf; for example, repo1 precedes repo2. Use --repo, such as --repo=1, to select a repository. Use --set to select a backup other than the latest.

For PITR with --type=time or --type=lsn, specify the target time or LSN with --target. Without --set, pgBackRest searches configured repositories in order for a backup containing the requested time or LSN. If none matches, --type=time uses the latest backup in the first repository that has backups. For --type=lsn, it selects no backup. For other PITR types, such as xid, use --set if the target precedes the latest backup. See Point-in-Time Recovery for details and examples.

item.title: pig ext
item.description:
pig ext searches the extension catalog and installs, updates, or removes PostgreSQL extension packages on the host. It also supports PostgreSQL server packages. After installing a package, apply the SQL and configuration required by the extension.

Command Description Notes
ext list Search extensions
ext info Show extension details
ext avail Show extension availability matrix
ext status Show host-visible extension files/packages Does not query every database
ext scan Scan installed control/library files Does not query every database
ext add Install extensions Requires sudo or root
ext rm Remove extensions Requires sudo or root
ext update Update extensions Requires sudo or root
ext import Download extensions for offline use Requires sudo or root
ext link Link a PG version into PATH Requires sudo or root
ext reload Refresh extension catalog

Quick Start

This example uses a running PostgreSQL 18 instance. To install and start one, follow Getting Started.

item.title: Server Command (server)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: server

The pgBackRest server allows access to remote hosts without using the SSH protocol.

Command Options

TLS Server Address Option (--tls-server-address)

TLS server address.

Set the IP address on which the server accepts client requests.

default: localhost
example: --tls-server-address=*

TLS Server Authorized Clients Option (--tls-server-auth)

TLS server authorized clients.

item.title: Roadmap
item.description:
Release Strategy

Pigsty uses semantic versioning: <major>.<minor>.<patch>. Alpha/Beta/RC versions will have suffixes like -a1, -b1, -c1 appended to the version number.

Major versions introduce incompatible foundational changes and major features. Minor versions usually add features and small API changes. Patch versions provide bug fixes and package updates.

Pigsty plans one major release per year and usually 4-6 minor releases. Minor releases generally follow PostgreSQL minor releases within one month. See Release Notes for the full history.

item.title: Join the Community
item.description:
GitHub

Find the project at github.com/pgsty/pigsty. You can support it with a star.

Contribute feature suggestions, new issues, or pull requests.

For documentation problems, submit issues to github.com/pgsty/pigsty.cc.

Press ⌘+ with K on macOS, or Ctrl+ with K, to search the documentation, extension catalog, and blog directly.

Maintainers

Pigsty is built by its maintainers and community.

item.title: pig build
item.description:
pig build downloads sources, installs dependencies, and produces RPM/DEB packages using Pigsty build recipes. Use it on an EL, Debian, or Ubuntu build host. Rust, pgrx, and the Xray client also support their respective macOS workflows.

Command Description Notes
build spec Initialize build specification directory
build repo Initialize required repositories Requires sudo or root
build tool Initialize build tools Requires sudo or root
build rust Install Rust toolchain Current user
build pgrx Install and initialize pgrx Current user
build proxy Set up Xray clients and servers Linux: root; macOS client: regular user
build get Download source tarballs
build dep Install extension build dependencies Requires sudo or root
build ext Build extension packages Current user
build pkg Complete pipeline: get, dep, ext Requires sudo or root

Quick Start

If the build host needs package repositories, run pig build repo. This backs up and replaces existing repository definitions. Skip this step if suitable repositories are already configured.

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.description:
Pigsty Software

For offline installation in a network-isolated environment, we receive no data about you.

During online installation, our servers or cloud provider servers log the requesting machine’s IP address and/or hostname and downloaded package names.

We will not share this information with other organizations unless required by law.

Pigsty’s primary domain is: pigsty.io. For mainland China, please use the registered mirror site pigsty.cc.

Pigsty Website

When you visit our website, our servers will automatically log your IP address and/or hostname in Nginx logs.

item.title: Server Ping Command (server-ping)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: server-ping

Ping a pgBackRest TLS server to check whether it accepts connections. This checks availability only; it does not attempt authentication.

If the command line does not specify a host, use tls-server-host.

Command Options

TLS Server Address Option (--tls-server-address)

TLS server address.

Set the IP address on which the server accepts client requests.

default: localhost
example: --tls-server-address=*

TLS Server Port Option (--tls-server-port)

TLS server port.

item.title: Stanza Create Command (stanza-create)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: stanza-create

After configuring a stanza in pgbackrest.conf, run stanza-create. With multiple repositories, pgBackRest creates the stanza in each one. It skips existing stanzas, so you can safely repeat stanza-create, including after adding a repository.

See Create the Stanza for more information and an example.

Command Options

Online Option (--online)

Create on an online cluster.

Specify –no-online to create the stanza without connecting to PostgreSQL.

item.title: pig sty
item.description:
pig sty installs Pigsty, prepares the controller, generates configuration, and runs deployment playbooks. It also manages dashboards through the Grafana HTTP API.

Command Purpose
sty init Download and extract Pigsty into an installation directory
sty boot Install Ansible dependencies and prepare the controller
sty conf Generate and validate an inventory from a template
sty deploy Run the deployment playbook
sty list / sty get List or download Pigsty releases
sty grafana Manage Grafana dashboards, language, and theme; alias gf

Quick Start

Run these commands on the controller:

item.title: Stanza Delete Command (stanza-delete)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: stanza-delete

The stanza-delete command removes repository data for a stanza.

WARNING:

Use this command with care. It permanently removes every backup and archive for the specified stanza from the pgBackRest repository.

To delete a stanza:

  • Shut down the PostgreSQL cluster associated with the stanza (or use –force to override).
  • Run the stop command on the host where the stanza-delete command will be run.
  • Run the stanza-delete command.

After the command succeeds, remove the stanza from all applicable pgBackRest configuration files and environment variables.

item.title: Subscription
item.description:
Pigsty combines tools from the PostgreSQL ecosystem with automated database management. It helps users use PostgreSQL, the world’s most popular database.

Pigsty resolves many PostgreSQL operational issues. Enterprise service quality also requires expert support and full coverage from the original provider. Pigsty Enterprise Edition adds these commercial services to the open-source edition. Choose services that meet your needs.

Consider a Pigsty subscription if you have any of these needs:

  • Run critical databases with strict SLA guarantees and full support coverage.
  • Get support for complex Pigsty and PostgreSQL issues.
  • Get guidance on PostgreSQL/Pigsty production practices.
  • Get expert help to interpret monitoring dashboards, identify performance bottlenecks and fault causes, and recommend actions.
  • Plan database architectures for security, disaster recovery, and compliance. Use your existing resources and business requirements.
  • Migrate other databases to PostgreSQL, or migrate and transform legacy instances.
  • Build observability systems, data dashboards, and visualization applications with Victoria/Grafana.
  • Move off the cloud to open-source RDS for PostgreSQL alternatives. Use solutions that are cloud-neutral and avoid vendor lock-in.
  • Get professional support for Redis/ETCD/Silo and extensions such as TimescaleDB/Citus.
  • Develop customized products and OEM branding with explicit commercial authorization.
  • Sell Pigsty as SaaS/PaaS/DBaaS, or provide technical services, consulting, and cloud services based on this distribution.

Subscription Plans

Pigsty offers the Open Source Edition and two subscription tiers. Choose Professional Edition or Enterprise Edition to meet your needs.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What is Pigsty, and what is it not?

Pigsty is a PostgreSQL distribution and a local-first, open-source RDS solution. It provides tools and operational practices for managing a DBMS. It is not itself a Database Management System (DBMS).

For comparison, a database is a car, a DBA is its driver, and RDS is a taxi service. Pigsty provides software to automate driving.

What problem does Pigsty solve?

Database operational expertise is scarce. Users can hire experts, rent managed RDS, or use Pigsty to automate database management. Pigsty helps users build efficient, high-quality local database services without a DBA, at less than 1/10 the cost of RDS.

item.title: pig inventory
item.description:
pig inventory (alias pig inv) inspects, edits, and validates the Pigsty inventory, pigsty.yml. It also checks deployment prerequisites and exchanges configuration with PostgreSQL through the experimental cmdb commands.

When you edit a fragment, PIG preserves the YAML content and formatting outside that fragment. Before saving, it parses the complete file again. If parsing fails or another process has changed the original file, PIG keeps the original and reports an error.

item.title: pig do
item.description:
pig do runs administration playbooks from the selected Pigsty directory. It uses the inventory to add clusters, create databases and users, install packages, or remove services.

Define the target configuration in the inventory first, then run the corresponding command. The commands invoke Ansible directly. This command group has no general --plan mode.

pig do pgsql-add pg-test 10.10.10.12 # add one PostgreSQL instance
pig do pgsql-rm pg-test 10.10.10.12 # remove one PostgreSQL instance
pig do pgsql-db pg-meta app # create or update a database
pig do pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_app # create or update a user
pig do node-pkg pg-meta restic # install a package on selected nodes
pig do redis-add redis-meta # initialize a Redis cluster

Inventory selection is shared with sty deploy. PIG passes the resolved source to Ansible without interpreting it again relative to Pigsty home. Missing explicit, environment, or default sources fail before playbook execution. Existing directory and executable Inventory sources remain Ansible inputs; static Inventory commands do not execute them.

item.title: pig postgres
item.description:
pig postgres (alias pig pg) manages local PostgreSQL instances and databases. Use it to initialize or control an instance, run SQL, maintain tables, and create database copies. Use pig pt for Patroni cluster operations and pig pitr for recovery with pgBackRest.

Commands run as the PostgreSQL operating-system user, normally postgres. Install PostgreSQL first. For a new data directory, make its parent writable by that user or create an empty directory with the correct ownership before running pg init.

item.title: Stanza Upgrade Command (stanza-upgrade)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: stanza-upgrade

Immediately after a PostgreSQL major version upgrade, update pg-path in all pgBackRest configurations to the new database location. Then run stanza-upgrade. It upgrades the stanza in every repository configured on the host. If the database is offline, use --no-online.

Command Options

Online Option (--online)

Update an online cluster.

Specify –no-online to upgrade the stanza without connecting to PostgreSQL.

item.title: Comparison
item.description:
Comparison with RDS

Pigsty is a local-first RDS alternative under Apache-2.0. You can deploy it on your physical machines, virtual machines, or cloud servers.

This comparison uses two benchmarks: Amazon AWS RDS for PostgreSQL and Alibaba Cloud RDS for PostgreSQL. AWS is the global market leader. Alibaba Cloud is the market leader in China.

Aliyun RDS and AWS RDS are closed-source cloud database services. You can only rent them on public clouds. The cloud-vendor information below is a February 2024 archive based on PostgreSQL 16. The Pigsty column in Feature Comparison follows the current release. The Key Extensions version table remains a historical snapshot.

item.title: pig patroni
item.description:
pig patroni (alias pig pt) runs the installed patronictl command. Use it to inspect cluster members, change cluster configuration, and switch the primary. PIG selects the configuration file and provides local service, status, and log commands. Other commands use patronictl’s arguments, prompts, output, and exit codes.

Install Patroni and configure access to its cluster before running cluster operations. Use pig pt COMMAND --help for native command help, or pig pt -- --help for patronictl root help. Running pig pt alone shows PIG’s help.

item.title: Start Command (start)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: start

After stop prevents pgBackRest processes from running, use start to permit them again. This does not immediately start any processes. See Starting and Stopping for details and examples.

General Options

Allow Run as Root Option (--allow-root)

Allow the command to run as the root user.

By default, only restore can run as root because it manages file ownership. Other commands can create root-owned files, for example in the repository. The PostgreSQL user cannot access these files, which causes later commands to fail.

item.title: pig pe
item.description:
Use pig pe to read metrics from a running pg_exporter and reload its configuration. The full command name is pig pg_exporter. Aliases are pe, pgexp, and pgexporter.

pig pe get # Show PostgreSQL metrics
pig pe list # List PostgreSQL metric families
pig pe stat # Show exporter statistics
pig pe reload # Reload exporter configuration

Select an exporter

The default endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:9630. Use these options to select another instance:

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html

This section answers common Patroni questions. Each subsection covers a different topic.

For more help or unexpected problems, see chatting and reporting_bugs.

Comparison with other HA solutions

Why does Patroni require a separate cluster of DCS nodes while other solutions like repmgr do not?
There are different ways of implementing HA solutions, each of them with their pros and cons.

Software like repmgr performs communication among the nodes to decide when actions should be taken.

item.title: pig pgbackrest
item.description:
pig pgbackrest (alias pig pb) creates backups, restores data, and manages pgBackRest stanzas. It runs pgBackRest as the PostgreSQL operating-system user, selected by --dbsu or $PIG_DBSU (default postgres).

Before the first backup, install pgBackRest and configure the stanza and repository in pgbackrest.conf. A stanza groups the backup configuration for one PostgreSQL cluster. In PostgreSQL, enable archive_mode and set archive_command to call pgBackRest.

Use pig pitr when recovery must also stop Patroni and PostgreSQL, then restart PostgreSQL. Use pig pb restore when you manage those steps yourself.

item.title: Stop Command (stop)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: stop

Prevent new pgBackRest processes from running. By default, existing processes can finish. Use --force to terminate them.

After stop completes, new pgBackRest processes return an error. See Starting and Stopping for details and examples.

Command Options

Force Option (--force)

Force all pgBackRest processes to stop.

Send TERM signals to all running pgBackRest processes for an immediate, graceful shutdown. This also stops processes started elsewhere that have remote processes on this host. For example, stop --force on the database server stops a backup that started on the backup server.

item.title: pig pitr
item.description:
Use pig pitr to restore a local PostgreSQL instance from pgBackRest backups. For a managed restore, PIG stops services as needed and restores the data. By default, it then starts PostgreSQL and leaves Patroni stopped for you to verify the recovered database.

Recovery replaces data in the target directory. Start with --plan to check the directory, backup source, recovery target, and service actions.

Before recovery

You need an installed pgBackRest, a readable configuration file, a usable backup, and the archived WAL needed to reach the target. The default config path is /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf. Select another file with -c and a stanza with -s.

item.title: Release notes
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releases.html

Version 4.1.5

Released 2026-08-12

Compatibility improvements

  • Compatibility with PostgreSQL 14.24, 15.19, 16.15, 17.11, 18.6 (Alexander Kukushkin)

    Add the new output_plugin_libraries GUC, which restricts logical decoding output plugins.

Improvements

  • Log REST API connection resets at DEBUG instead of WARNING (Kyle McLaren)

    Ensure the common “client went away mid-write” variants are silenced without affecting the handling of genuine (non-connection) errors.

Bugfixes

  • Fix thread_stack_size validation alignment (Sundong Kim)

    Changed aligned from 65535 to 65536 in the thread_stack_size schema. Previously, patroni --validate-config rejected almost all realistic values, including the daemon default 524288.

  • Allow validation of synchronous_mode to accept 'quorum' and boolean-like strings (Eray Araz)

    patroni --validate-config previously rejected synchronous_mode values such as quorum and the PostgreSQL-style boolean strings that are accepted at runtime.

item.title: Verify Command (verify)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: verify

Verify checks whether repository backups and archives are valid.

Command Options

Output Option (--output)

Output type.

The following output types are supported:

  • none - No verify output.
  • text - Output verify information to stdout.
default: none
example: --output=text

Set Option (--set)

Backup set to verify.

item.title: Version Command (version)
item.description:
Source: pgBackRest Command Docs: version

Display the installed pgBackRest version.

Command Options

Output Option (--output)

Output type.

The following output types are supported:

  • text - Display the installed pgBackRest version as text.
  • num - Display the installed pgBackRest version as an integer.
default: text
example: --output=num

item.title: meta
item.description:
The meta configuration template is the default Pigsty template. It deploys PostgreSQL on one node, which is the core function of Pigsty.

For compatibility across operating system distributions and architectures, meta installs only the minimum required software.

  • Description: Default single-node installation template with extensive configuration parameter descriptions and minimum required feature set.
  • OS Distro: el8, el9, el10, d12, d13, u22, u24, u26
  • OS Arch: x86_64, aarch64
  • Related: meta, slim, fat

Usage: This is the default template. You do not need to specify -c meta during configure:

item.title: rich

Use this template to build a local software repository, use Silo backup storage, or run Docker applications. It also provides preconfigured business databases.

item.title: mssql
item.description:

Since v4.2, Pigsty builds Babelfish directly and does not use the WiltonDB repository. Babelfish is available on all supported Linux platforms.

For the complete tutorial, see: Babelfish (MSSQL) Kernel Guide

item.title: Supported Linux
item.description:
Pigsty runs on Linux with amd64/x86_64 and arm64/aarch64 architectures. It supports three major distribution families: EL, Debian, and Ubuntu.

Pigsty runs directly on the host without containers. It supports actively maintained mainstream releases in these three families on both architectures.

RHEL / Rocky / Alma 10 aarch64 el10.aarch64

RHEL / Rocky / Alma 9 aarch64 el9.aarch64

Ubuntu 26.04 (resolute) aarch64 u26.aarch64

item.title: File Hierarchy
item.description:
Pigsty FHS

The default Pigsty home directory is ~/pigsty. It has this file structure:

- app/ {open=false}
 - Application template resources
- bin/ {open=false}
 - Management and operations scripts
- files/
 - victoria/ {open=false}
 - Rules and operations scripts
 - grafana/ {open=false}
 - Grafana dashboards
 - postgres/ {open=false}
 - PostgreSQL management scripts
 - migration/ {open=false}
 - Data-migration task definitions
 - pki/ {open=false}
 - Self-signed CA and certificates
- roles/ {open=false}
 - Ansible role implementations
- templates/ {open=false}
 - Ansible templates
- vagrant/ {open=false}
 - Vagrant sandbox definitions
- terraform/ {open=false}
 - Terraform cloud-resource templates
- configure
- ansible.cfg
- pigsty.yml
- *.yml

/infra is a runtime symlink to /data/infra. This directory contains observability data and generated configuration:

item.title: PostgreSQL Mongo Mode
item.description:
The mongo configuration template is a PostgreSQL deployment mode, not an independent Pigsty module. It combines:

  • PostgreSQL 18 managed by the standard PGSQL module
  • The documentdb extension and its required preload libraries
  • A stateless FerretDB proxy deployed with Pigsty’s Docker APP workflow

PostgreSQL manages all data, high availability, backups, monitoring, and the database lifecycle. FerretDB provides only the MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint.

Quick Start

The default template is a single-node deployment on 10.10.10.10. FerretDB listens on loopback by default.

item.title: Applications
item.description:
Pigsty applications have two categories:

  • Software Templates: Docker Compose templates under ~/pigsty/app/<name> for stateless business components.
  • Data Applets: PostgreSQL + Grafana analytics demos, mainly for learning and showcase use.

Application Model

The recommended application deployment workflow is:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap
./configure -c <template> # e.g. app/dify, app/immich, app/jumpserver, app/maybe, supabase
vi pigsty.yml # edit passwords, domains, IPs, and secrets
./deploy.yml # deploy infrastructure and databases
./docker.yml # install Docker
./app.yml # launch applications

app.yml copies app/<name> templates to /opt/<name>. It replaces .env with apps.<name>.conf, then runs docker compose up -d.

item.title: Enterprise Self-Hosted Supabase
item.description:
Pigsty can deploy Supabase on your physical, virtual, or cloud servers with a single command. Self-hosting provides more extensions, performance options, control, and potential cost savings.

As of August 2026, the official Supabase self-hosting guide recommends Docker and classifies other implementations as community projects. Pigsty is an independent community integration and is not currently listed on that page.

This tutorial requires basic Linux knowledge. Otherwise, consider using Supabase cloud or plain Docker Compose self-hosting.

item.title: Odoo: Self-Hosted Open Source ERP
item.description:
Odoo is open-source ERP software with CRM, sales, inventory, and other business applications. The template stays on Odoo Community 19.0 for addon compatibility and uses PostgreSQL 18.

Odoo 19 requires PostgreSQL 13 or later and Python 3.10 or later; the official Docker image provides Python.

Quick Start

On a fresh Linux x86_64 / ARM64 server running a compatible operating system:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap # Install Ansible
./configure -c app/odoo # Generate the Odoo configuration
vi pigsty.yml # Change default passwords
./deploy.yml # Install Pigsty and PostgreSQL
./docker.yml # Install Docker Compose
./app.yml # Initialize the Odoo database and start the web container

Port 8069 is published on all host interfaces by default. Open http://<ip>:8069. The initial application login is admin / admin; change the password at first login.

item.title: Dify: AI Workflow Platform
item.description:
Dify is an open-source platform for developing generative AI and LLM applications. It supports agent creation, AI workflows, RAG retrieval, and model management. These features help users build and operate generative AI applications.

Pigsty supports self-hosted Dify with single-command deployment. Critical state resides in externally managed PostgreSQL. You can use pgvector in the same PostgreSQL instance as the vector database to simplify deployment.

  • Quick Start
  • Why Self-Host
  • Installation
  • Configuration
  • Checklist
  • Domain and SSL
  • Upgrading
  • File Backup

The template uses Dify v1.17.1 with plugin daemon v0.6.10-local and sandbox v0.2.15. Validation on 2026-10-08 covered login, an existing Code workflow, and service connections on Linux amd64 with PostgreSQL 18.6. Dify v1.16 and later handle PostgreSQL 18’s built-in uuidv7() without a local migration patch.

item.title: InsForge: AI Backend-as-a-Service
item.description:
InsForge is an open-source Backend-as-a-Service platform for AI coding agents, built around PostgreSQL. It provides authentication, database APIs, file storage, a model gateway, edge functions, site deployment, and payment integrations. These features reduce common backend implementation work.

Pigsty provides the app/insforge template. It runs stateless InsForge OSS services in Docker Compose and stores critical state in Pigsty-managed PostgreSQL. This provides high availability, backup and recovery, monitoring, ingress domains, and infrastructure services. The database does not depend on an ephemeral container volume.

item.title: Hindsight: AI Long-Term Memory
item.description:
Hindsight is a PostgreSQL-native long-term memory service for AI agents.

Pigsty provides the app/hindsight configuration template (conf/app/hindsight.yml). By default, it uses Pigsty-managed PostgreSQL instead of Hindsight’s built-in development database.

Quick Start 

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap
./configure -c app/hindsight
vi pigsty.yml # edit domain, database password, and LLM settings
./deploy.yml
./docker.yml
./app.yml

Default access URLs:

  • UI: http://hs.pigsty or http://<IP>:9999
  • API: http://hs-api.pigsty or http://<IP>:8888

Key Settings

conf/app/hindsight.yml overrides /opt/hindsight/.env through apps.hindsight.conf. Key parameters:

item.title: FerretDB: MongoDB Protocol
item.description:
FerretDB provides a MongoDB-compatible protocol over PostgreSQL and the DocumentDB extension. Pigsty’s app/ferretdb runs the stateless protocol proxy. PostgreSQL, the postgres database, DocumentDB extensions, and a backend PostgreSQL login role must already exist. The fork/mongo configuration template prepares these dependencies together.

Quick Start 

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap
./configure -c fork/mongo
./deploy.yml
./docker.yml -l pg-meta
./app.yml -l pg-meta

Install mongosh or another MongoDB-compatible client separately. Then connect with the dedicated login from the template:

item.title: NocoDB: Open-Source Airtable
item.description:
NocoDB is an open-source Airtable alternative that turns any database into a smart spreadsheet.

Use its visual interface to create database applications without code. NocoDB supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, and other databases. You can use it for internal tools and data management systems.

Quick Start

Pigsty provides a Docker Compose configuration file for NocoDB in the software template directory:

cd ~/pigsty/app/nocodb

Review and modify the .env configuration file (adjust database connections as needed).

Mattermost is an open-source team collaboration platform and a private alternative to Slack.

item.title: Wiki.js: OSS Wiki Software
item.description:
Public Demo: http://wiki.pigsty.cc

The current Compose uses the untagged requarks/wiki image. Stable 2.x releases are maintained in requarks/wiki-v2; the original requarks/wiki repository contains 3.x Beta releases. The image resolved to 2.5.316 during validation on 2026-10-08. Record and verify the actual image version before production upgrades.

TL; DR 

cd ~/pigsty/app/wiki && docker compose up -d

Postgres Preparation 

# postgres://dbuser_wiki:DBUser.Wiki@10.10.10.10:5432/wiki
- { name: wiki, owner: dbuser_wiki, revokeconn: true , comment: wiki the api gateway database }
- { name: dbuser_wiki, password: DBUser.Wiki , pgbouncer: true , roles: [ dbrole_admin ] }
bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_wiki
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta wiki

Configuration 

services:
 wiki:
 container_name: wiki
 image: requarks/wiki
 environment:
 DB_TYPE: postgres
 DB_HOST: 10.10.10.10
 DB_PORT: 5432
 DB_USER: dbuser_wiki
 DB_PASS: DBUser.Wiki
 DB_NAME: wiki
 restart: unless-stopped
 ports:
 - "9002:3000"

Access

  • Default Port for wiki: 9002
infra_portal:
 wiki: { domain: wiki.pigsty.io, endpoint: "127.0.0.1:9002" }
./infra.yml -t nginx_config,nginx_reload -l infra

Kernel Templates pgsql, pg19, mssql, polar, ivory, agens, pgedge, mysql (OpenHalo), mongo, pgtde, oriole

item.title: Maybe: Self-Hosted Personal Finance
item.description:
Maybe is an open-source personal finance application. It manages accounts, transactions, budgets, investments, and household financial views. This Rails application stores production business data in PostgreSQL and uses Redis for background job queues.

Pigsty’s app/maybe template connects stateless Maybe Web / Worker containers to Pigsty-managed PostgreSQL. Local Redis provides the Sidekiq queue. Financial data resides in a PostgreSQL cluster with backup, monitoring, and recovery support, rather than an ephemeral Docker volume.

item.title: Immich: Self-Hosted Photo and Video Library
item.description:
Immich is a high-performance, self-hosted photo and video management application. It is a popular open-source alternative to Google Photos, licensed under AGPL-3.0. Features include web and mobile uploads, album sharing, timelines, maps, EXIF and RAW support, and LivePhoto. It also provides semantic search, facial recognition, and automatic backups.

Pigsty’s app/immich template runs the Immich application layer with Docker Compose and stores metadata in Pigsty-managed PostgreSQL. The template follows Immich v3 and uses VectorChord by default for similar-image search, smart search, and face-search vectors. On 2026-10-08, both Server and ML images resolved to 3.3.0. Validation used a new media library on Linux amd64 with PostgreSQL 18.6 and covered uploads, thumbnails, and real machine-learning inference.

make

  • Proxy HTTPS: 8443
  • Admin API: 8001

bin/pgsql-db pg-meta kong

item.title: ha/octo
item.description:
ha/octo builds a compact high-availability simulation with the first eight nodes from vagrant/spec/deci.rb. It exercises co-located modules, VIPs, remote backup, and larger membership counts. Do not use it directly as a production blueprint without reviewing capacity, security, and failure domains.

Overview

  • Config name: ha/octo
  • Node addresses: 10.10.10.10 through 10.10.10.17
  • INFRA: 3 nodes. Only the first builds and serves the local repository. As the comments describe, Docker can be installed separately on all three nodes.
  • ETCD: 5 nodes on the last five hosts
  • Object storage: one eight-node, single-drive cluster. The template does not override minio_type. Thus, deployment and removal both default to Silo. Before removal, verify this value, the exact target, and the data paths.
  • pg-meta: 3-node PostgreSQL cluster with VIP 10.10.10.2/24
  • pg-test: 5-node PostgreSQL cluster whose final instance has the offline role, with VIP 10.10.10.3/24
  • Backup: uses the object-storage repository through sss.pigsty:9002 and also retains a local repository
./configure -c ha/octo
./deploy.yml

This template depends on fixed eight-node addresses and VIPs. For another environment, update the host addresses, VIPs, interfaces, DNS, and repository node together. Also change every public example credential.

item.title: Metabase: BI Analytics Tool
item.description:
Metabase is an open-source business intelligence tool. Teams can quickly explore and visualize data through its interface without SQL knowledge.

Metabase provides many chart types and connects to different databases. These features support enterprise data analysis.

The template defaults to metabase/metabase:v0.64.1.x. Use the single METABASE_IMAGE setting to override the full image reference. On 2026-10-08, the tag resolved to 0.64.1.1; validation on PostgreSQL 18.6 covered upgrading a restored metadata database, login, and querying an existing saved question.

item.title: Registry: Container Image Cache
item.description:
Pigsty provides the app/registry template (conf/app/registry.yml) for:

  • Docker Registry cache service (default 5000)
  • Optional management UI (default 5080)

The default images are registry:3.1.2 and joxit/docker-registry-ui:2.6.0. The template is a pull-through cache for one upstream, Docker Hub by default. This mode does not accept image pushes.

Quick Start 

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap
./configure -c app/registry
vi pigsty.yml # update domains, certs, and ports if needed
./deploy.yml
./docker.yml
./app.yml

Default endpoints:

item.title: JumpServer: Open-Source Bastion Host
item.description:
JumpServer is an open-source PAM and bastion-host system. It manages centralized access to SSH, RDP, database, and web assets. Pigsty’s app/jumpserver template runs Community Edition application containers with Docker Compose. Pigsty-managed PostgreSQL provides persistent database storage.

The template uses JumpServer v5.0.0-ce. It retains Community Edition core, celery, koko, kael, chen, and web services, plus local Redis. It removes the upstream installer’s built-in PostgreSQL service. Pigsty manages PostgreSQL, backups, monitoring, Nginx ingress, and the database lifecycle.

item.title: ha/full
item.description:
The ha/full template defines the recommended Pigsty sandbox. It deploys two PostgreSQL clusters on four nodes for tests and feature demonstrations.

Most Pigsty tutorials and examples are based on this template’s sandbox environment.

  • Description: Four-node complete feature demonstration environment with two PostgreSQL clusters, Silo, Redis, etc.
  • OS Distro: el8, el9, el10, d12, d13, u22, u24, u26

  • OS Distro: el8, el9, el10, d12, d13, u22, u24, u26

item.description:
Electric is a PostgreSQL sync engine. It delivers database changes efficiently to frontend and edge applications.

Pigsty provides the app/electric template (conf/app/electric.yml). It configures the database, containers, and ingress in one workflow.

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty

./deploy.yml

  • http://elec.pigsty (default domain in the template)

Metrics port defaults to 8003 (ELECTRIC_PROMETHEUS_PORT).

item.title: Jupyter: Notebooks and Data Analysis
item.description:
JupyterLab is an interactive notebook, terminal, and data-analysis environment. Pigsty v4.5.0 has two distinct deployment paths:

  • The VIBE module, managed by Ansible and systemd, for the complete v4.5.0 development sandbox.
  • The lightweight standalone app/jupyter Docker Compose template documented here.

app/jupyter is not a default apps inventory entry. Prepare its data directory separately. app.yml -e app=jupyter does not handle directory ownership.

Quick Start 

cd ~/pigsty/app/jupyter
vi .env # change JUPYTER_TOKEN and optionally pin JUPYTER_IMAGE
chmod 600 .env
make dir # create /data/jupyter, owned by 1000:100
make up # docker compose up -d

Generate a strong token with openssl rand -hex 32. The default port is 8888; open http://<host_ip>:8888.

item.title: ha/dual
item.description:
The ha/dual template deploys one primary and one standby on two nodes. This Semi-HA configuration provides limited failover when only two servers are available.

Overview

  • Config Name: ha/dual
  • Node Count: Two nodes
  • Description: Two-node limited HA deployment, tolerates specific server failure
  • OS Distro: el8, el9, el10, d12, d13, u22, u24, u26
  • OS Arch: x86_64, aarch64
  • Related: ha/trio, slim

Usage:

./configure -c ha/dual [-i <primary_ip>]

After configuration, replace 10.10.10.11 with the standby node’s actual IP address.

item.title: ha/citus
item.description:
The ha/citus template deploys a Citus distributed PostgreSQL cluster. It has 1 infrastructure node, 1 coordinator group, and 5 worker groups. The coordinator and worker groups contain 12 Citus nodes in total. The cluster distributes data into shards and supports horizontal scaling.

Overview

  • Config Name: ha/citus
  • Node Count: 13 nodes (1 infra + 1 coordinator×2 + 5 workers×2)
  • Description: Citus distributed PostgreSQL HA cluster
  • OS Distro: el8, el9, el10, d12, d13, u22, u24, u26
  • OS Arch: x86_64
  • Related: meta, ha/trio

Usage:

item.title: PGLOG: PostgreSQL Log Analysis Application
item.description:
PGLOG is a sample Pigsty application that uses pglog.sample in MetaDB as its data source. Load logs into this table, then open the related dashboard.

Pigsty provides commands to retrieve CSV logs and load them into the sample table. These shortcuts are available on the meta node by default:

catlog [node=localhost] [date=today] # Print CSV log to stdout
pglog # Load CSVLOG from stdin
pglog12 # Load PG12 format CSVLOG
pglog13 # Load PG13 format CSVLOG
pglog14 # Load PG14 format CSVLOG (=pglog)

catlog | pglog # Analyze current node's log for today
catlog node-1 '2021-07-15' | pglog # Analyze node-1's csvlog for 2021-07-15

Use these links to view the sample log analysis:
